questions.question_text: Which test is most direct for determining whether the series Σ (n=1 to ∞) 1/n² converges?
questions.explanation: This is a p-series with p = 2 > 1, so it converges immediately by the p-series test. The ratio test is inconclusive here (limit equals 1) — a classic trap: the ratio test fails on every p-series.

questions.question_text: The series Σ (-1)ⁿ/√n converges conditionally. What does "conditionally" mean here?
questions.option_a: It converges only for certain values of n
questions.option_b: It converges, but the series of absolute values Σ 1/√n diverges
questions.option_c: It converges to a value that depends on the order of terms only if p > 1
questions.option_d: It diverges unless grouped in pairs
questions.explanation: Conditional convergence = the alternating series converges (by AST) while Σ|aₙ| = Σ 1/n^(1/2) is a divergent p-series (p = 1/2 ≤ 1). The exam tests whether you check BOTH the series and its absolute version.

questions.question_text: The Maclaurin series for eˣ is Σ xⁿ/n!. What is the coefficient of x³ in the Maclaurin series for x·e^(2x)?
questions.explanation: x·e^(2x) = x·Σ (2x)ⁿ/n! — the x³ term comes from x times the (2x)²/2! term: x · 4x²/2 = 2x³, so the coefficient is 4/2 = 2. The trap is substituting 2x but forgetting the extra factor of x shifts every power up by one.

questions.question_text: A curve is defined by x(t) = t², y(t) = t³ − 3t. What is dy/dx at t = 1?
questions.explanation: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = (3t² − 3)/(2t). At t = 1: (3 − 3)/2 = 0. Students who differentiate y with respect to x directly, or invert the quotient, get C. Parametric slopes are always a quotient of t-derivatives.

questions.question_text: What is the total area enclosed by the polar curve r = 2cos(3θ)?
questions.explanation: A rose r = a·cos(3θ) has 3 petals. One petal spans θ ∈ [−π/6, π/6]: area = ½∫4cos²(3θ)dθ = π/3. Three petals → π. The trap: integrating 0 to 2π double-counts because the curve traces each petal twice over a full revolution.

questions.question_text: Which technique most directly evaluates ∫ x·eˣ dx?
questions.explanation: A polynomial times an exponential is the signature setup for integration by parts: u = x, dv = eˣdx gives xeˣ − eˣ + C. u-substitution fails because the derivative of eˣ doesn't produce the lone x factor.

questions.question_text: ∫ dx/(x² − x) is best evaluated by rewriting the integrand as:
questions.explanation: x² − x = x(x − 1), and partial fractions gives 1/(x(x−1)) = A/x + B/(x−1) with A = −1, B = 1. Check by recombining: [−(x−1) + x]/(x(x−1)) = 1/(x(x−1)) ✓. Option A has the signs flipped — always verify by recombining.

questions.question_text: For which value of p does ∫ (1 to ∞) 1/xᵖ dx converge?
questions.explanation: ∫₁∞ x⁻ᵖ dx converges exactly when p > 1. Note the mirror-image rule: ∫₀¹ x⁻ᵖ dx converges when p < 1. Mixing up which side needs p > 1 is one of the most common BC errors.

questions.question_text: Given dy/dx = x + y with y(0) = 1, what is the Euler's method estimate of y(0.2) using step size 0.1?
questions.explanation: Step 1: slope at (0, 1) is 0 + 1 = 1, so y(0.1) ≈ 1 + 0.1(1) = 1.1. Step 2: slope at (0.1, 1.1) is 0.1 + 1.1 = 1.2, so y(0.2) ≈ 1.1 + 0.1(1.2) = 1.22. The trap is reusing the old slope for the second step — Euler's method re-evaluates dy/dx at each new point.

questions.question_text: A population follows dP/dt = 0.4P(1 − P/600). What is the population when it is growing fastest?
questions.explanation: Logistic growth is fastest at half the carrying capacity: L/2 = 300. The carrying capacity (600) is where growth approaches zero — choosing it confuses 'largest population' with 'fastest growth.'

questions.question_text: Which integral gives the arc length of y = x² from x = 0 to x = 1?
questions.explanation: Arc length = ∫√(1 + (dy/dx)²)dx with dy/dx = 2x, so the integrand is √(1 + 4x²). Option A squares the function instead of its derivative; option B forgets to square 2x.

questions.question_text: The series Σ (n=1 to ∞) n!/nⁿ converges. Which statement best explains why the ratio test proves this?
questions.option_c: n! grows slower than nⁿ for all n, so terms go to 0
questions.option_d: The limit of aₙ₊₁/aₙ is e > 1
questions.explanation: aₙ₊₁/aₙ = (n+1)!·nⁿ / (n!·(n+1)ⁿ⁺¹) = (n/(n+1))ⁿ = 1/(1+1/n)ⁿ → 1/e ≈ 0.37 < 1. Note C is true but insufficient — terms going to 0 never proves convergence (harmonic series!).

questions.question_text: A particle's position is r(t) = ⟨t², sin t⟩. What is its speed at t = 0?
questions.explanation: Velocity = ⟨2t, cos t⟩ = ⟨0, 1⟩ at t = 0; speed = √(0² + 1²) = 1. Speed is the magnitude of velocity — answering 0 comes from looking only at the x-component.

questions.question_text: Using the Lagrange error bound, the maximum error when approximating sin(0.1) by the first-degree Maclaurin polynomial P₁(x) = x is at most:
questions.explanation: |R₁| ≤ M·|x|²/2! where M bounds |f''| = |−sin| ≤ 1, giving (0.1)²/2 = 0.005. The sharper bound (0.1)³/6 applies because P₁ = P₂ for sine — but the question asks for the standard first-degree Lagrange bound, n+1 = 2. Read which n the bound uses.

questions.question_text: ∫ ln x dx equals:
questions.explanation: Parts with u = ln x, dv = dx: x ln x − ∫x·(1/x)dx = x ln x − x + C. Option A confuses integration with differentiation; option D incorrectly treats ln x like a power of x.

questions.question_text: The area inside the cardioid r = 1 + cosθ is:
questions.explanation: A = ½∫₀²π (1+cosθ)² dθ = ½∫(1 + 2cosθ + cos²θ)dθ = ½(2π + 0 + π) = 3π/2. The cos² term contributes π (average value ½ over a full period) — dropping it gives the wrong answer π.

questions.question_text: The general solution to dy/dx = ky is y = Ceᵏˣ. If y(0) = 5 and y(2) = 20, then k =
questions.explanation: C = 5, then 20 = 5e²ᵏ → e²ᵏ = 4 → k = (ln 4)/2 = ln 2. Both expressions are equal: (ln 4)/2 = (2 ln 2)/2 = ln 2. The exam loves equivalent log forms — simplify before eliminating.

questions.question_text: ∫₀¹ 1/√(1−x) dx is:
questions.explanation: The integrand blows up at x = 1, making this improper. lim(b→1⁻) [−2√(1−x)]₀ᵇ = 0 − (−2) = 2. This is the p < 1 case at a finite endpoint, which converges. Don't confuse it with π/2, which belongs to ∫1/√(1−x²).

questions.question_text: The power series Σ (x−3)ⁿ/(n·2ⁿ) has radius of convergence 2. Its interval of convergence is:
questions.explanation: Center 3, radius 2 → endpoints 1 and 5. At x = 5: Σ 1/n diverges (harmonic). At x = 1: Σ (−1)ⁿ/n converges (alternating harmonic). Always test endpoints separately — the ratio test says nothing there.

questions.question_text: The length of the curve x = cos t, y = sin t for 0 ≤ t ≤ π/2 computed by the parametric arc length formula is:
questions.explanation: L = ∫√((dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²)dt = ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin²t + cos²t) dt = ∫₀^(π/2) 1 dt = π/2 — a quarter of the unit circle, as geometry confirms. When the integrand simplifies to 1, trust it; students often second-guess clean results.
